title: Growth by conquest
hook: Republican conquest became imperial rule, then reached Britain and the eastern theatres.
notes: Historical locations are approximate city/site anchors, not surveyed battle sites or territorial polygons. No modern state is used as a proxy for Roman sovereignty. Events follow cited ancient accounts and institutional histories; ancient authors are not neutral eyewitnesses to every event. BC dates use astronomical years internally. Met: The Roman Republic and The Roman Empire; English Heritage for AD 43. Historical geometry fallback: georeferenced Mitchell 1880 map, inset removed; its provincial divisions and colouring are retained as historical cartography, not authoritative boundaries. Credit: David Rumsey Map Collection, David Rumsey Map Center, Stanford Libraries. Adaptation CC BY-NC-SA 3.0.

scenes.title: Conquest before emperors
scenes.text: The republic acquired territory by war and diplomacy. Its final civil wars culminated in Caesar’s dictatorship and assassination in 44 BC.

scenes.title: A new kind of ruler
scenes.text: In 27 BC Octavian became Augustus. Move the timeline from the republican crisis to imperial rule: power changed at Rome before the empire’s outer geography stopped changing.

scenes.title: Across a channel, beyond a river
scenes.text: Britain’s conquest began in AD 43. Under Trajan, war extended into Dacia and Parthia. These widely separated anchors show theatres of expansion rather than implying a continuous surveyed border.

scenes.title: How an atlas imagined the empire
scenes.text: Mitchell’s 1880 atlas reconstructed Rome at its greatest extent. The cleared historical overlay offers an empire-wide view; it is a nineteenth-century interpretation with approximate georeferencing, not an exact AD 117 boundary. Adjust its opacity to compare coastlines.
